A FIELD GUIDE TO YOUR EXPLORATION

Start with a question.

When did atoms form? Where did carbon come from? Why does every galaxy see expansion? Use the chapters, element atlas and laboratory to explore these questions. This is an educational reconstruction; animations illustrate ideas, rather than predict particle trajectories or individual galaxies.

ControlsGlossaryAccess & languagePrivacy & offline use

Explore at your own pace

  • History: choose a chapter or use Previous and Next. Play history advances through the chapters and stops at today. The time slider compresses the enormous gaps between epochs.
  • 3D view: drag to orbit, or focus the canvas and press arrow keys. Zoom with the + and − buttons, keyboard +/−, or mouse wheel. Reset view restores the camera.
  • Periodic table: search by English name, symbol or atomic number. Aluminum, cesium and sulphur are accepted spelling variants. Press Enter in search to select the first match; Escape clears the search. Search highlights matches while retaining every element's position.
  • Keyboard: Tab moves between controls. Left/Right moves through elements in atomic-number order; Up/Down moves to the nearest element in the same displayed column. Home/End goes to the first/last element. Enter or Space selects. Tab after an element reaches its scrollable details. In the matter tabs, use arrows to move focus and Enter or Space to open a panel.
  • Small screens: swipe the periodic table horizontally. Element details are below it and scroll separately when necessary.
  • Expansion laboratory: increase the scale factor and change the observer. Distances grow proportionally from every reference galaxy. This uses a fixed comparison value of H₀, not a simulation of the changing expansion rate.
  • Particle processes: choose a process, then play it or move its progress slider. The 3D view above shows the reaction. Switching away pauses it. Playback also pauses when this browser tab is hidden.

A small scientific glossary

Scale factor, a
The relative size of cosmic separations in the homogeneous model, normalized to 1 today. A value of 0.5 corresponds to half the present separation for objects following the expansion.
Redshift, z
The fractional stretching of light's wavelength. For cosmological expansion in this model, 1 + z = 1/a.
CMB
Cosmic microwave background: relic thermal radiation from the early universe. Its temperature is different from the temperatures of stars and gas.
ΛCDM
A cosmological model with a cosmological constant (Λ) and cold dark matter (CDM). The simulation also includes ordinary matter and radiation.
Mpc
A megaparsec is one million parsecs, approximately 3.26 million light-years. km/s/Mpc expresses recession speed per unit separation.
Atomic number and isotope
Atomic number counts protons. Isotopes of an element share that count but have different numbers of neutrons. Element production pathways depend on the isotope.

Access and language

The interface and scientific content are currently in English. Browser translation may help, but it has not been reviewed for scientific accuracy. Calculated numbers automatically use your browser’s regional decimal and grouping conventions. This does not translate text or static scientific equations.

Use browser zoom to enlarge text. Controls have keyboard focus indicators. Playback starts only when requested, and reduced-motion preferences disable smooth scrolling and transitions. If WebGL is unavailable, the timeline, element atlas, laboratory values and notebook remain usable. The notebook and this guide can also be read with JavaScript disabled.

These features support access; they do not constitute a certified accessibility conformance claim.

Privacy and offline use

This version has no accounts, analytics, advertising, tracking cookies or external application dependencies. The application does not save preferences in browser storage. Previously saved number-format preferences are no longer used.

Open the downloaded application's index.html to use the local simulation offline. Visiting a hosted copy once does not guarantee that it will remain available offline. The evidence links lead to external sites and need an internet connection; those sites apply their own privacy practices. A hosting provider may collect ordinary access logs independently of this application.
